title: NURS 1017 Unit 7 Case Study 11

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Nurses' Notes. Highlight the findings that require follow-up.
question.explanation:
Require follow-up: a shuffling, wide-based, “magnetic” gait, two falls and a Timed Up and Go of 28 seconds (high fall risk, especially living alone on two floors); new urinary urgency and incontinence; and slowed thinking, apathy and forgetfulness. Together these are the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus: gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline.

Do not require follow-up now: hearing aids and past cataract surgery are part of her history (the nurse checks that they are working, since poor hearing and vision add to fall risk). No resting tremor and no headache are pertinent negatives: they make Parkinson disease and a raised-pressure problem less likely.

leftContent.intro: The nurse in a neurology clinic is caring for a 74-year-old female client who is accompanied by her daughter.

question.stem: The daughter asks whether her mother has dementia or Parkinson disease. For each finding, click to specify whether it is most consistent with normal pressure hydrocephalus, Alzheimer disease, or Parkinson disease.

rows.text: Walking improves after some CSF is removed by lumbar puncture
Memory loss is the first problem; walking stays normal until late in the disease
Resting tremor, rigidity, and slow movement
Wide-based, “magnetic” gait with urinary incontinence early in the illness
Enlarged ventricles with no blockage of CSF flow
Gradual loss of recent memory, getting lost in familiar places, and repeating questions

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Diagnostic Results.
question.explanation:
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH): CSF builds up in the ventricles because it is not absorbed well, but the pressure measured by lumbar puncture is normal or only slightly raised. The enlarged ventricles stretch the nerve fibres that run past them to the legs and bladder and frontal lobes, causing the gait, bladder and thinking changes. Improvement after removing CSF (tap test) suggests she will benefit from a shunt. NPH is one of the few treatable causes of cognitive decline, which is why recognizing it matters.

Alzheimer disease begins with memory loss; gait and continence stay normal until late. Parkinson disease causes a resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and a shuffling, narrow-based gait.

Types of hydrocephalus: non-communicating (obstructive), when CSF flow is blocked inside the ventricular system (for example, a narrowed cerebral aqueduct or a tumour); communicating (non-obstructive), when CSF flows freely but is not absorbed by the arachnoid villi (for example, after meningitis or a subarachnoid hemorrhage); and normal pressure hydrocephalus, a form of communicating hydrocephalus in older adults.

question.explanation:
Risk for falls is the priority: a fall could cause a hip fracture or head injury (and older adults with enlarged ventricles are at risk of subdural bleeding). Her gait, two recent falls, a slow Timed Up and Go and living alone on two floors make a fall likely.

Urinary urgency sends her rushing to the bathroom, often at night, which is a common time for falls. A toileting schedule, a night light, a commode near the bed and grab bars reduce both incontinence and falls. Her slowed thinking makes it harder for her to remember safety measures, so her daughter is included in the plan.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the client's plan of care after shunt insertion? Select all that apply.

options.text: Press the shunt valve behind her ear every hour to keep it working
Assess the abdomen for pain, distension and bowel sounds
Have her lie on her right side so the valve stays warm
Walk with her using a gait belt, and offer the toilet every 2 hours
Restrict her fluid intake to reduce CSF production
Compare each neurological check with her baseline before surgery
Inspect the head and abdominal incisions and the skin along the shunt tract for redness, swelling or drainage
Include her daughter in teaching about the shunt

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 15 1500 and the Provider Orders.
question.explanation:
Include: comparing neurological checks with her baseline detects early problems (bleeding, shunt malfunction). The incisions and the tunnelled path of the tubing under the skin (head, neck, chest, abdomen) are checked for infection or CSF leakage. The lower end of the shunt drains into the peritoneal cavity, so abdominal pain, distension or absent bowel sounds are reported. Early, assisted walking and scheduled toileting address her fall risk and urgency. Her daughter will help watch for problems at home.

Do not include: the valve is pumped only if the neurosurgeon orders it. Lying on the valve side puts pressure on the incision and valve; she is positioned off the operative side as ordered. Fluid restriction does not change CSF production and risks dehydration, constipation and delirium.

leftContent.intro: The nurse in a neurology clinic is caring for a 74-year-old female client who is accompanied by her daughter.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give her a large meal to settle her stomach before she leaves
Perform and document a full neurological assessment
Tell the daughter to watch her mother and call if she is not better in a few days
Tell the emergency team about the recent MRI and the programmable valve
Keep her lying down with the head of the bed raised and stay with her until transport arrives
Contact the neurosurgery team now and arrange urgent transport to the emergency department
Press the shunt valve several times to restart the drainage

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Week 6 1100 and the Vital Signs from Week 6 1100.
question.explanation:
Return of her gait, bladder and thinking problems with new drowsiness, headache, vomiting, a slower pulse and a higher BP suggests shunt malfunction with rising pressure. Here the MRI may have changed the setting of her programmable valve (the magnet of an MRI scanner can reset some valves).

Correct: shunt malfunction is urgent: the neurosurgery team is contacted and she is assessed in hospital (valve setting check, imaging). The nurse reports the MRI and the valve type. A full neurological assessment gives a baseline for the emergency team. Keeping her in bed with the head raised and staying with her prevents falls and aspiration if she vomits.

Incorrect: waiting risks a serious decline. She is vomiting and drowsy, so she is not given food (aspiration risk, and she may need a procedure). The nurse does not pump the valve without an order.

leftContent.intro: The nurse in a neurology clinic is caring for a 74-year-old female client who is accompanied by her daughter.

question.stem: For each statement, click to specify whether it indicates an understanding of the teaching or a need for further teaching.

rows.text: Daughter: “Before any MRI, we'll tell the staff she has a programmable shunt so the setting can be checked afterwards.”
Client: “Now that I have the shunt, I don't need my walker or the grab bars any more.”
Daughter: “If she gets sleepy, has headaches or vomiting, or her walking gets worse again, we'll call neurosurgery right away.”
Daughter: “Redness or fluid along the tubing, a fever, or pain in her belly needs to be reported.”
Client: “The shunt is permanent, so I won't need any more check-ups.”
Client: “I'll carry the card that says what kind of shunt valve I have.”

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Week 6 1700 and Month 3 1000.
question.explanation:
Understanding: programmable valves can be changed by strong magnets (MRI, some magnetic toys or devices held to the head), so staff must know and the setting is checked after an MRI. Return of NPH symptoms, drowsiness, headache or vomiting can mean shunt malfunction; fever, redness or fluid along the tubing, or abdominal pain can mean infection. A shunt card gives emergency staff the valve details.

Needs further teaching: her walking has improved, but she should keep using her walker and home safety measures until physiotherapy advises otherwise; falls remain a risk. A shunt needs lifelong follow-up because it can block, break, become infected or drain too much or too little.
